thread.title: After the Bell: The Dow Needed a Reason to Drop 170 Points Today. It Got Two.

author: Ben Levisohn, Jon Swartz and Teresa Rivas
title: After the Bell: The Dow Needed a Reason to Drop 170 Points Today. It Got Two.
text:
More tariff talk hit the , because of course it did. In today's After the Bell , we...
•...explain why markets might be heading higher anyway;
•...consider what Dropbox's IPO could mean for Silicon Valley's unicorns;
•...take a look at the impact of wage hikes on retailers like Gap (GPS).
There's Always a Reason for the Market to Drop
Just when you think the market has reached escape velocity , something happens to knock it back down again. Look no further than today for an example.
The market opened up this morning but that was as good as it got. The S&P 500 declined 0.6%, to 2,765.31, today, while the fell 171.58 points, or 0.7%, to 25,007.03. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1%, to 7511.01. It's enough to make me think my call for new highs in the Dow and the S&P 500 from this past weekend is just plain wrong.
But maybe not. Stephen Todd at Todd Market Forecast contends that when the market is in an uptrend, like it is now, it often takes some sort of catalyst to knock it down. Today we had two: the abrupt departure of Rex Tillerson as Secretary of State and reports that the Trump administration is planning new tariffs on China . Those seemed to overshadow a benign inflation report this morning. "We barely missed getting our stop hit on our trading position.... I do believe that we have a good chance to hold on," Todd says. "In other words, I suspect that the pullback is almost over."
Let's hope so. — Ben Levisohn
Dropbox: Getting Ready for the Drop
File-sharing company Dropbox is being closely watched as a litmus test for the fortunes of tech IPOs in 2018 after a prolonged dry patch. Investors, already understandably anxious, might check their pulses after Dropbox said it is going public at a valuation well below the $10 billion it was assessed at after its last private funding round.
Illustration: Bloomberg News The Silicon Valley unicorn is targeting a public market capitalization of $6.3 billion to $7.1 billion in its IPO, according to a filing on Monday. Restricted stock units put the range at $6.7 billion to $7.6 billion.
The disparity between public market expectations and private valuations underscores the premium that private investors have put on dozens of unicorns, several of which are prime IPO candidates this year and in 2019.
Perhaps none has higher aspirations than Dropbox, which boasts strong revenue growth and a robust customer base. Company co-founder Drew Houston famously turned down an acquisition offer from then- Apple (AAPL) CEO Steve Jobs in 2009.
Dropbox’s revenue soared 30% last year to $1.1 billion from $845 million in 2016. That helped the company narrow net losses to $112 million from $210 million. The company has more than 500 million registered users, 11 million of which pay for premium features.
The company, which aims to raise up to $648 million by going public, would be one of the largest U.S. IPOs by an enterprise tech company since 2015 if it reaches the high end of its offering stock price of $16 to $18 per share. — Jon Swartz
Maybe Wage Increases Aren't So Bad After All?
Wage growth is supposed to be bad for retailers, but so far that hasn't been the case. An increase in lower-income workers' earnings can even be beneficial for companies like AutoZone (AZO), Target (TGT), and Walmart (WMT), even if they raise their own employees' pay.
Illustration: Pixabay The companies themselves don't seem to be too worried. Barclays' Chethan Mallela, for instance, notes that Michael Kors (KORS), Ralph Lauren (RL), and Tapestry (TPR) did not cite wage pressure on their earnings calls, suggesting that companies with "accessible luxury" business models, sizable wholesale operations (for the former two), and more international exposure are faring better in the current environment.
But wage increases aren't hitting even the companies you'd expect it to. Gap (GPS), for instance, doesn't appear to be seeing wage pressure even though it seems like a more obvious candidate to be squeezed. Investors, however, seem to be treating it as if wage increases are just around the corner, Mallela says, hence Gap's only modest outperformance since its strong fourth-quarter results earlier this month. That's created a buying opportunity, in his opinion.
Maybe investors listened: Gap gained 1.3%, to $32.67 today, while the SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT) dropped 0.2%, to $45.19. — Teresa Rivas
